methods.label: Minimize the digit count, then the arrangement
methods.explanation:
Divisibility by \(9\) depends on the digit sum, and each digit \(9\) contributes a multiple of \(9\). Let \(f\ge1\) be the number of 4s and \(g\ge1\) the number of 9s. The digit sum is \(4f+9g\), so \(4f\) must be divisible by \(9\). It is also a positive multiple of \(4\). The least common multiple of \(4\) and \(9\) is \(36\), so
\[
4f\ge36,\qquad f\ge9.
\]
Thus every eligible number has at least ten digits. A ten-digit candidate must have exactly nine 4s and one 9.

Divisibility by \(4\) depends only on the last two digits, because all earlier digits contribute a multiple of \(100\). Among the possible endings \(44,49,94,99\), only \(44\) is divisible by \(4\). Therefore the last two digits must be \(44\).

Among ten-digit candidates, keeping earlier digits equal to \(4\) makes the number smaller. Place the single \(9\) as far right as permitted, in the hundreds place. This gives
\[
n=4444444944.
\]
Its digit sum is \(45\), and it ends in \(44\), so it satisfies both divisibility conditions. Shorter numbers are impossible, longer numbers are larger, and this is the smallest allowed ten-digit arrangement. Its last four digits are \(4944\), choice \(C\).
